newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Funds braced for equity slowdown, no panic.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Funds braced for equity slowdown, no panic.

text.p: Global money managers are braced for a softer showing from major bond and equity markets, but few see any factors likely to upset their longer term strategies.

They said concerns about value in the U.S. and European stock markets were key short term factors in allocation strategies currently, but felt that the markets would be back on track by the New Year at the latest if a correction did come through in the coming weeks.

A Reuters poll of mostly London-based managers showed a lightening of North American equity holdings on average, an increase in UK equity holdings and a continued reduction in Asia ex-Japan by global equity fund managers. The poll also showed an increased average Japanese weighting.
Mike Grimble, investment strategist at Norwich Union, told Reuters he expected a pullback of about 10 percent in the U.S. over the next six months.

"We are not that bothered about inflation so we don't see any major triggers for a marked downturn, but a certain amount of rationality ought to return to the markets. We see it drifting lower over the next few months with no major dramatic sell off."

The U.S. and Canada were weighted at 27 percent in August, down from 27.5 percent in July. Latin America and other emerging markets were down from July at 5.7 percent but still up from the levels seen earlier in the year.
Shaun Roache, strategist at ING Barings, said high valuations in the U.S. and Europe were forcing investors to look elsewhere, but there was no cause for concern about a major correction.
"The outlook is more difficult but maybe the movement we have been seeing is a bit exaggerated," he said.
Roache said transaction costs outweighed the benefits of going into cash at the moment considering that a major earnings or interest rate induced correction on Wall Street is unlikely.
"Although the outlook is more difficult it certainly isn't the kind of terrain that would encourage us to raise cash at the moment."

The poll showed an increased taste for British equities in global equity and UK pension funds. The average weighting in UK equities in global equity funds was 12.0 percent against 10.3 percent in July, and in pension funds 57.2 percent from 56.6 percent.
UK pension funds also upped their weighting in overseas equities to 22.9 percent from 22 percent.

Tony Robinson, head of equities at Lombard Odier, said the firm was not making any major allocation changes, and was happy to be fully invested unless a stable U.S. and German interest rate outlook changed.
Lombard Odier had sold some holdings in Latin America and some U.S. blue-chips in the last two weeks, but was looking to re-invest that "not too far below current levels".

The global bond fund showed an increased average cash weighting, reflecting concerns about low yield in the major markets. The cash weighting rose to 6.9 percent from 4.6 percent in July at the expense of the U.S. and Europe ex-Germany and France.

Juan Nevado, strategist at Prudential Portfolio Managers, said many markets -- bond and equity -- were offering no risk premium. "When you buy risk assets you expect to be given a risk premium and some of these assets don't have a risk premium."
He said Prudential had been reducing equities and becoming more liquid in recent months, buying cash and cash proxies like index linked bonds.

"We have been cutting back on Europe over the last few months where we think the markets are most vulnerable," he said, adding that UK looked cheaper than some core European markets such as Germany, France and Switzerland.
"We think the obvious value plays at the moment are places like the UK and Japan. We like Mexico, which is actually a relatively cheap market...(and) Australia is much cheaper than the U.S."
Grimble said Norwich Union was keeping a reasonable weighting in property, and internationally Japan offered value.

Roache said ING Barings was steering clear of South East Asia with currency volatility clouding equity market prospects, while eastern and Mediterranean European markets' low or sometimes negative correlations with the U.S. offered respite when the U.S. entered a period of renewed volatility.
